records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 20 Deutsche Bank AG Twin Deficit Model Framework: We use the budget deficit and the current account deficit to construct the twin deficit (TD), equally weighted. Both are from the IMF's WEO. Our twin deficit score TDS(t) is a weighted average of recent years' TD, i.e., TD(t), TD(t-1), …, TD(t-5), assigning a larger weight to the most recent print. We also incorporate the cumulative sum of TD of previous years. That allows to capture both the flow and stock characteristics of this variable. We then run daily regressions of each year's TDS vs 10y EGB spreads to Bund. The regression excludes Italy, Portugal and Ireland. These daily regressions generate time series of the slope (proxy for market price of risk), the constant, and the residuals of each country's spread. records.text: 423/02/2026 France leading the pack in AI-related FDI: Despite policy uncertainty, the past year showed France to be an attractive destination for AI-related investment. According to UN data, data centres accounted for a large share of global foreign direct investment (FDI) in 2023, and France led the pack with USD69bn of inbound FDI, followed by the US (USD29bn) and South Korea (USD21bn). All other countries attracted less than USD10bn AI investment each (Figure 9). The bulk of this inflow stemmed from mega-projects, notably the United Arab Emirates’ commitment of more than USD43bn and Canada’s USD16bn, which are together expected to create roughly 6,000 jobs. The Trump administration has already decided to apply Section 122 tariffs up to 15%, an increase from the initially stated 10% and above the current 14% effective tariff rate. For context, Section 122 allows tariffs as high as 15% on countries with trade deficits with the US for up to 150 days without congressional approval. Section 122 is expected to act as an interim measure while the Trump administration considers other options. For example, the administration may invoke Section 301, allowing the President to impose tariffs on countries found to engage in unfair trade practices, pending a USTR investigation. Section 338 authorizes retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% against nations discriminating against US businesses, with the President bearing the burden of proof. Alternatively, Section 201 permits action but only after review by the independent US International Trade Commission (USITC). Each of these tariff measures can be challenged in the Court of International Trade (CIT). Finally, President Trump is expected to continue, and possibly expand, Section 232 tariffs, which target specific industries and are harder to challenge because they relate to national security. records.text: European Economic Perspectives23 February 2026 ab 10 As regards labour income, Cazzaniga et al. (2024) outline three transmission channels. First, AI could replace workers by shifting tasks from labour to AI capital, thus leading to a reduction in labour income. Second, AI might push up income of workers that are not replaced, particularly in AI-related sectors. Third, broader AI-related productivity gains could lead to higher aggregate incomes, offsetting income losses from displacement of some workers. This implies that the overall impact on income levels and the distribution will depend on the net impact of gains from stronger economic activity and labour income losses. However, sector employment data currently does not indicate any significant shifts due to AI. All in all, we think that, while the near-term implications for employment and incomes in Europe are likely to be relatively limited, AI will still play an increasingly important role over the longer term. Our estimate of "core" tariffs (ex fuels, gold and AI-related imports) is closer to 13-14%. If Section 122 tariffs were not extended by Congress, the tariff level would fall to mid single digits, ~6%-7%. The mid- single-digit range ex-Section 122 may be a floor for tariffs in the medium term. As for a tariff ceiling, raising tariffs to levels comparable to the "risk" scenarios from around Liberation Day last year is now quite complicated. Reliance on section-based tariffs and/ or Congress will complicate the path to higher tariffs and reinforces our argument for a pivot from country to sector tariffs. records.text: E M – L O CA L E YE S F O R A G L O B A L V IEW 225/02/2026 Our aggregation of the ‘general account’ assets of 11 domestic life insurers shows that holdings of domestic bonds fell by JPY2,486.6bn on a market-value basis in Q3 of FY2025, while holdings of foreign bonds rose by JPY1,611.2bn. Even on a book-value basis, the three categories – policy-reserve-matched bonds, held-to-maturity (HTM) bonds, and other securities – shrank across the board. The total unrealised loss on JPY-denominated bonds in these categories amounted to JPY22.6trn; lifers appear to be swapping higher-book-value bonds for lower-book- value ones in order to reduce that loss. When a heavily undervalued off-the-run JGB is exchanged for a near-par current bond, the transaction results in a net sale on a face-value basis and a reduction in book-value holdings. For super-long JGBs, some issues have become severely under-par, prompting concerns about impairment. Under the prevailing accounting standards, a security that has an unrealised loss of 50% or more will be impaired unless recovery can be demonstrated. With HTM sovereign bonds, an insurer could argue that the price will recover if the bond is held to maturity. Nevertheless, in October 2025 the Accounting Standards Board of Japan released a draft amendment stating that HTM securities will not be subject to mark-to-market impairment testing. records.text: Scenario 1: We see a 1pp potential LCR uplift from reclassification of GSE securities as Level 1 HQLA Currently, GSE securities (Fannie/Freddie) are classified as Level 2A HQLA. If recast as Level 1, the 15% haircut they receive when calculating HQLA would be removed, which would result in up to 1%/1pp increases to HQLA/LCRs across the banks. Most banks do not break down the composition of level 2A HQLA between GSE and other qualified securities. As such, we use the ratio of disclosed total balance of FNMA securities vs. other foreign debt securities in Y-9C filings to estimate the implied portion of reported L2A consisting of FNMA/FHLMC securities. While the impact to LCRs is not material, partially given that banks have remixed security portfolios from MBS into UST over recent years, we believe that if Fannie and Freddie securities were re-classified as level 1 HQLA, banks could rebalance portfolios back towards MBS over time, increasing the LCR impact. Market Structure: BDCs, Credit Funds and MM CLOs in perspective The private credit market is roughly $2tn AUM, with $1.5tn invested. BDCs account for one-third of invested assets ($0.5 tn), with one-third in public vehicles treated as permanent capital despite share volatility across the broader asset class. Private BDCs ($325bn) carry greater redemption risk, but only represent about 22% of the ~1.5tn in invested capital in private credit. With recent BDC disclosures suggesting average outflows in the mid-single-digit context, this equates to approximately 1% of total private credit assets. Redemptions can be met through cash, inflows, loan sales, or proration, a likely outcome for many nontraded BDCs in 2026 . Private credit and debt funds represent nearly 60% of private credit assets, totaling ~$960bn. Most capital here is long-term and locked up, with limited annual redemption windows or rollover options, providing investor flexibility without systemic instability. Finally, middle-market CLOs represent roughly 10% (~$140 billion) of invested capital. These are permanent, hold-to-maturity structures where investor behavior is primarily ratings-driven and based on underlying portfolio performance. records.text: GBP By-election time The Gorton and Denton by-election on Thursday is this week's main focus in the UK. The obvious risk is that PM Starmer may not be able to survive a heavy loss in an erstwhile safe seat, but a loss in the election should not be taken for granted. The more fundamental issue remains that the so-called soft left wing of the Labour party has increased its influence, which we think justifies a higher fiscal premium in the pound. By how much is unclear at the moment, as the ultimate outcome is very much path dependent, but a c.0.87 EURGBP premium is far from excessive and we retain short GBPAUD exposure. Last week's data were encouraging in the aggregate, with flash PMIs, fiscal performance, retail sales and a still-sticky domestic inflation backdrop all pointing to a healthier underlying demand situation than the continuous pickup in the unemployment rate might hint at. That said, Catherine Mann reiterated her concerns regarding labour market softness, which arguably brings the March cut – and potentially more further out – a step closer. A number of MPC members are due to appear this week, including Governor Bailey. Commodity FX CAD's cross-currents; renewed Antipodean divergence Its sizable rally versus the dollar notwithstanding, the CAD continues to underperform other commodity currencies because of continued geopolitical friction with the US. We maintain that the NT is (strategically) following the same play book it has followed in the last couple of years : prudence in February’s national budget, followed by a further outperformance on budget consolidation in the mid -term budget (see South Africa 2926 budget preview: Anchor down , dated 17 February). It is also worth pointing out that ZAR20bn in additional tax measures that were assumed in the 2025 MTBPS have been removed in today's budget, pushing down its overall buoyancy assumptions. This to accounts for the bulk of slippage in the headline deficit and, in fact, marks the first time since 2020 and Covid-19 that the NT has assumed a weaker rather than stronger main budget revenue performance. Critically from an optics perspective too, non-interest expenditure changes were very limited (flat growth over the next three years), clearly showing little to no evidence of any shift towards populist spending into local elections (see below). In recent years, we find that (upward) revenue adjustments to the budget framework have generally outstripped (or at the very least matched) any decision to raise non -interest spending (Figure 1). This is clear evidence of the NT taking its credibility clawback seriously. We believe today’s budget also raises the chances of earlier credit ratings upgrades by rating agencies later this year. Preference to keep flattening the curve ; extend target

Even though total defense expenditures are rising significantly, they still lag behind the again significantly increased budget targets. Also, total federal investment spending (excl. the KTF) increased noticeably over the year. Still, the January reading looks stronger at first glance than it really is. In this context, it is worth noting that the overall strong increase in core budget investment spending should not obscure the fact that it was exclusively due to higher financial aid – and here, in particular, to further federal loans to social security institutions. Even though these loans are counted as investments in a financial statistical context (in contrast to the national accounts), they do not strengthen the public capital stock and thus the growth potential of the economy. Even though ongoing non-financial hurdles (planning, approval, and implementation delays) argue against a full achievement of the ambitious expenditure targets this year, the continued increases in defense and investment are likely to be large enough to drive the general government deficit (federal government, states, municipalities, social security funds; national accounts definition) noticeably higher, from 2.4% of GDP in 2025 to a forecast 3.5% of GDP in 2026. By contrast, net trading profits were dragged down by worsening unrealised losses on bonds, which have accumulated as rates have risen. City banks’ deposit–loan gap has begun to narrow. Loan books are expanding steadily, while deposits are still growing but not at the same pace, and in some cases they are even declining. Historically, the deposit–loan gap has been viewed as the pool of funds that banks can use to purchase JGBs. In the long-lasting deflationary era, the gap kept widening, giving the impression that Japanese banks had virtually unlimited funding to buy JGBs. However, the QQE that followed replaced much of the banks’ JGB holdings with BoJ reserves, meaning that, for a while, banks could simply draw down these balances to buy more bonds. Figure 14: Going with the liquidity flow Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg This should support continued ample system liquidity, which our corporate bond flows seem to be confirming. Looking at the relative flows into high yield relative to IG activity puts us into a +2.5 STD range, which historically has not occurred without supportive liquidity (Figure 14). And while we think the Fed’s RMP changes in December was partially a result of the ability of liquidity to make it into the parts of the market with the most funding stress, current credit spreads defacto support the view tha t they are flowing into the corporate bond space. Conclusion: Our key takeaway is that the belief that AI will cause widespread business destruction is premature. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 19 Higher tariff risk stems from an escalation in Section 301 tariffs on China. A large portion of Chinese imports (over 70%) currently face Section 301 tariffs, which were put in place in 2018-19. The President has the discretion to modify these tariffs, and if the administration were to raise these tariffs by 10%, it would raise tariffs on consumer categories by up to 2%. This number, at the moment, is quite modest given the share of imports from China has collapsed in 2025, from 13% to as low as 7%. If imports from China were to retrace higher, the impact would be proportionately higher as well. Our Public Policy team believes Section 232 (National Security-based tariffs) to be less of a threat for most core consumer goods. Further, even if investigations are announced, these would likely take several months to be completed, and there are no consumer goods-focussed Section 232 tariffs ongoing, as we discuss in previous sections. New Section 301 investigations at a country-level are a risk, these will likely take closer to a year to be completed. Taken together, we see risks on tariffs to consumer goods skewed lower in the near, medium and long term, although the range of magnitudes is wide and uncertainty remains high.

records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 79 EUR STIR: Assessing factors behind ECB cut pricing The market is pricing around 8bps of cuts in total from the ECB, the most seen since the start of the year. From a timing perspective, the trend of pushing back the trough towards the end of the year has continued. Looking at meeting dates, the bulk of cuts occur over the second half, with a premium for forecast meetings observed (Sept in particular). This does not adjust for the risk of the estr-depo spread tightening over the course of the year, which would underestimate the extent of cut pricing marginally. Over the past year we have assessed ECB pricing against three factors - USD pricing, commodity and currency developments (proxied by oil in euros), and data surprises. When updating this, a couple of observations stand out. The decoupling of pricing from USD markets over the second half of 2025 we think can be explained by it being driven by idiosyncratic expectations over the incoming Fed Chair. But more recently it appears USD pricing has been more influential, as the market has latched on to concerns over AI . It also does appear that the market has looked through developments in the energy complex; though this is likely to reflect the kneejerk reaction to newsflow around potential tariffs at the beginning of the year. Energy infrastructure is not the primary objective, but the scale of operations results in a material, localised disruption to Iran’s export chain. Banks are not permitted to assume access to the discount window in their own internal liquidity modeling, which we believe has resulted in banks operating at higher buffers to their LCR requirements, in certain cases. In our view, and as discussed in industry publications (see here), one potential solution would be to allow banks to include some benefit for the pre-pledged borrowing capacity in their LCR calculations. We estimate that if 50% of the estimated pre-pledged discount window capacity were included as inflows within the NCO component of LCR, this could add up to 29pp of LCR upside across the top 7 banks (Exhibit 11). The structure of LCR calculations limit the amount of HQLA at bank subsidiaries that banks can include in their holding company LCRs: The operating structure of most US banks consists of a holding company (holdco), and a main operating subsidiary bank n (bank sub), which contains the majority of the holdco’s assets and profitability, and both holdco and bank subs have LCR requirements. However, a bank may only include eligible excess bank sub HQLA in holdco LCR calculations up to the amount of the bank n sub’s NCO, unless the excess is freely transferable from the bank sub to another legal entity.1 Simplistically, the bank cannot include the vast majority of bank sub excess HQLA in its holdco LCR in excess of the bank sub’s standalone 100% LCR requirement. US investors reacted sharply to the muddied USD outlook in 2025 by reducing their hedges on overseas assets from over 25% in early 2025 to below 12% by the end of the year. They have continued the process in 2026, with the US foreign hedge ratio now at 11.3%, its lowest since 2011. Overseas investors to the US were, in contrast, reluctant to increase USD hedges in 2025, presumably deterred by the cost of protecting against dollar weakness. The start of 2026 has, however, seen them start to increase hedges more consistently. Foreign hedge ratios into the US are now close to 59%, up from below 53% at the start of December. There is a plausible argument that the scale of AI and its speed of adoption increase the likelihood that it will be a substitute for labour, at least in the short term. Moreover, the labour market will most likely lag financial markets if there are risks of a significant disruption. This tempers the comfort one takes from resilient data. There are valid counterarguments, such as “speed bumps” in the adoption of AI due, for instance, to regulation, accountability or validation processes. However, irrespective of the right answer, the uncertainty by itself may be enough to dampen demand in the short term. Longer term, however, one should be sceptical of statements that technological progress will result in structurally low inflation. Technological progress primarily changes relative prices. General inflation will, as always in a world of fiat money, be determined by the fiscal and monetary policy mix. In the current environment, it is unlikely that the “substitute” scenario will prove to be politically sustainable. It should trigger significant fiscal support for unemployment on top of the long list of desired fiscal spending: energy independence, critical minerals, AI investments, defence, and providing support for an ageing population. Groq’s LPUs are designed to prioritize sequential processing, enhance compute density, and optimize memory bandwidth, which minimizes inefficiencies and maximizes throughput for LLM inference. The company claims its chips can run LLM models up to ten times faster and use a tenth of the energy compared to current alternatives for inference. This chip uses 1/3 of the energy per token of a GPU and Groq believes that over a 3-year period the chips would break even with the energy costs alone of an NVIDIA GPU. Groq is able to do this in part by using shorter, thinner wires which results in less energy expenditure as data moves through the chips. In December 2025, it was reported that NVIDIA is buying assets from Groq for $20bn, with the goal of integrating Groq’s low-latency processors into the NVIDIA AI factory architecture. records.text: Net Upside Geopolitical Risks Given the market focus on Iran, we first provide key statistics around supply from Iran and flows via the Strait of Hormuz, and then present scenarios, illustrating the two-sided but net upside risks to our oil price forecast. We think of Iran-related oil disruption scenarios as either reductions in Iran oil supply only, or scenarios where broader regional oil production or shipping is negatively affected. Key Stats Around Supply From Iran and Flows Via the Strait of Hormuz Iran crude production has risen by 1.4mb/d over the last 5 years, and has stabilized around 3.5mb/d over the last year (Exhibit 11).6 Iran production remains currently largely unaffected by the recent geopolitical developments. Iran’s oil production is highly concentrated in the southwest (near the Iraq and Kuwait borders), except for the very large South Pars field, which accounts for over 1mb/d of Iran oil production, jointly owned by Iran and Qatar. Iran exports about half of its domestic crude production (mostly to China), with nearly all exports by sea. Iran’s exports are highly concentrated in the Kharg Island export terminal, which accounts for over 90% of Iran seaborne exports (Exhibit 12). Iran has a Goreh-Jask pipeline on the Gulf of Oman, designed to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, with capacity estimates ranging from 0.3mb/d to 1mb/d, which is reportedly not used for crude exports. 6 Iran also produces about 0.8mb/d of condensate. records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 38 Deutsche Bank AG Gilt H6-M6 futures roll We provide an overview of the upcoming Gilt futures roll, focusing on its fair value and potential trading strategies. Our views on the roll are primarily driven by our estimated fair value, current market positioning, and other associated risks. We anticipate that the majority of the futures roll will take place between Thursday, 19th February, and the first notice day on Thursday, 26th February. Both the front and back contracts currently share the same CTD bond, which is 1E39. Holding the front contract's CTD represents a positive carry position, while the implied repo rate is higher at the start of the delivery period. This implies that shorts will optimally deliver on Monday, 2nd March. As of 13th February, our indicator suggests a neutral positioning in the market. Our models suggest the fair value of the switch option is 0.25p for the M6 contracts, with negligible switch optionality for the H6 contract. The most probable alternative CTD for both the front and back contracts is 4T38, which would occur at lower yields. The roll's fair value is approximately 1p lower than the current market level. Therefore, given the neutral positioning and close-to-fair-value market pricing, we are neutral on the G-H6G-M6 futures roll. records.text: Noel Dixon 23 February 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Trump IEEPA tariffs struck down by SCOTUS: Now What? The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) has rendered its decision, officially invalidating President Trump’s application of tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). So, what comes next? The administration retains several alternative options, including recourse to Section 122, Section 201, Section 301, Section 338, as well as the potential for expanded use of Section 232. Nevertheless, these alternative measures impose greater limitations on Trump regarding tariff rate caps and the criteria needed to apply tariffs, especially compared to the more flexible IEEPA. In many instances, the Trump administration must initiate investigations through bodies such as the International Trade Commission, the Commerce Department, or the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR). At present, there are hundreds of tariff refund lawsuits pending in the US trade court, which will likely require a significant amount of time to resolve. The SCOTUS ruling notably omitted this aspect, leaving it to lower courts to address. We believe the effective tariff rate will remain relatively unchanged in the short term. However, due to the current constraints on the President, changes could occur over the medium term, affecting fiscal and inflation projections and impacting certain countries more than others. records.text: New US “global tariff” 4. To replace the tariffs imposed under the IEEPA, President Trump announced a 10% “global tariff” under Sec. 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 shortly after the Supreme Court ruling. On Feb. 21, President Trump announced he was raising the new global tariff to 15%, but as of this writing he has not signed a new executive order to implement this and the details of the change are not yet clear. Tariffs imposed under Sec. 122 are limited under law to a maximum rate of 15% and can last for up to 150 days “unless such period is extended by an act of Congress.” The new “global tariff” is subject to very similar exemptions as the previous reciprocal tariff and would thus apply to around 50% of US imports from the EU and around 60% of US imports from the UK. Sectoral tariffs imposed under Sec. 232 will remain in place, while other goods — including energy products and pharma—will remain exempted. 5. On net, our US colleagues have estimated that a new 15% global tariff net of exemptions would raise the US effective tariff rate on the EU by 7.8pp (vs. a 6.9pp reduction due to the IEEPA ruling) and by 8.7pp in the UK (vs. a 5.8pp reduction due to the IEEPA ruling). The recent tariff news thus implies a net increase in the US effective tariff rate on the EU of 0.9pp to 12.1% and a net increase of 2.9pp to 10.9% for imports from the UK2. This marks a break with the past because, historically, EM local debt has delivered low Sharpe ratios and a high correlation to a traditional 60:40 portfolio, implying a limited role in global portfolios (see Figure 1). KEY MESSAGES The distinction between emerging markets and developed markets is becoming increasingly blurred, driven by convergence in fiscal, external vulnerability, monetary policy credibility and improving liquidity. This convergence supports a structurally positive case for EM, suggesting EM rates and FX should have a larger share of global portfolios. We expect this convergence to lead to structurally increased inflows into EM FX and rates, higher volatility-adjusted returns and more diversification benefits. Technical factors, such as abundant USD liquidity and developed local derivatives markets, will continue to support inflows into EM local bonds, in our view, making them a more ‘hedge-able’ asset class. Bilateral trade deals to stay in place for now So far, existing bilateral agreements between the US and Asian economies, including last year’s US-China arrangements and the most recent US-India trade deal, remain intact for now. No partner government has signaled any intention to withdraw from these frameworks in response to the Supreme Court ruling. However, the medium-term outlook remains uncertain. As new sector-specific Section 232 and Section 301 tariffs begin rolling out later this year, volatility in trade flows may return. Trump’s China visit to shift to non-tariff issues The SCOTUS ruling has significantly altered the policy backdrop for the planned state visit on March 31st – April 2nd. Because tariff levels are now driven primarily by US domestic statutory processes rather than bilateral negotiations, the upcoming visit is unlikely to involve new tariff announcements. In H1 2025, asset managers flipped from an overweight to a significant underweight in the USD, especially those based outside the US. In theory, it should take incrementally negative news on the US economic or policy outlook to produce a materially weaker USD. The tariff disruption, or the tech rotation if it remains that, does not warrant such news. The pattern of USD flows in the run‑up to the Supreme Court announcement was nevertheless revealing. The continuation of USD selling in aggregate was led by forward USD sales from US‑based investors, which is significant as their underweight had been much reduced at the end of last year and therefore has room to extend once again. We also observed increased forward USD sales related to US equity hedging, another area where non‑US investors had room to extend their USD shorts. So, while this is not the regime change in USD sentiment observed in February and March 2025, it is still consistent with investors extending USD shorts where there is room to do so. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Before diving in, however, we would like to clarify a key point: while an outright and sustained closure of the Strait of Hormuz is not impossible, we do not include it as a core scenario. The threshold for such an outcome is high and the likelihood appears very low. The US Fifth Fleet is headquartered in Bahrain with a longstanding remit to protect freedom of navigation, and the US and its allies maintain extensive air and maritime capabilities (including mine countermeasures) that would make a prolonged closure difficult to sustain. A closure attempt would also be economically self damaging for Iran, given its own exports rely on these waters, and would directly jeopardise flows to key customers such as China - factors that would likely galvanise a broad multinational response. Consistent with historical experience, we therefore focus on scenarios that range from de escalation to limited frictions, localised Iranian export-chain disruption, and transit impairment via operational and shipping constraints (rather than sustained closure). dministration has other options for trade actions that could be applied quickly, such as import licenses. They also have other authorities under which they could impose tariffs, though the other provisions come with procedures such as investigations or hearings, or limits on the magnitude of tariffs and time period for which tariffs can remain in place. Using section 301, the administration would have a wide bandwidth to impose tariffs at the country level. Ultimately, the administration can likely replicate the "deals" on a more permanent basis through section 301 over time and can also impose sectoral tariffs through existing section 232 investigations with little lift. This could mean that the administration still leverages negotiating power with trading partners. We'd note that while there is potential for further legal challenges to the administration's use of section 122, recent challenges to section 301 tariffs did not prove successful, nor have various challenges to section 232 tariffs. See a summary from the CRS here. The shift from IEEPA to provisions with a clearer legal track record and delegation from Congress for use to impose tariffs could ultimately lead to a more durable tariff structure in the medium term. In the interim for a better understanding of the potential moving parts for plan B please see last week's US Economics Weekly, here. Agreement between State Street’s Foreign Exchange Holding Indicator (FXHI) and Foreign Exchange Hedge Ratio Indicator (FXHRI) enhances a positioning-driven view for developed market currencies. Because the impact of flows on future returns also depends on the positions of institutions in that currency, the FXHRI is, with the FXHI, designed to quantify and measure empirically this aspect of investor behaviour. The indicator is updated on a daily basis with a two -day publication lag. We publish foreign currency hedge ratios against multi-asset portfolios and are able to disaggregate this multi -asset hedge ratio into hedges against equity assets and fixed income assets. FX Behavioural Factor Flows and Factor Holdings measure real-money demand for and positioning in FX factors. At a high level, the indicators reveal whether real -money investors are leaning into or leaning out of a given FX factor (e.g. carry, value, momentum). The indicators aggregate single currency indicators, including the Foreign Exchange Flow Indicator (FXFI) and Foreign Exchange Holdings Indicator (FXHI), into broader factor aggregates. records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 61 UK Gilt Issuance We provide the upcoming gilt auction calendar together with cash flow dynamics for the next quarter. In the UK, there will be an auction of conventional 4.125% Mar 2033 next week. In the following week, there will be an auction of conventional 4% Mar 2029. records.text: ab 23 February 2026 Global Research Global Strategy AI Disruption: Are we heading for a credit crunch? Executive summary: BDC redemptions, outflows raise odds of a credit crunch Recent headlines on BDC redemptions have heightened concerns about forced selling and potential spillover effects. In summary, AI disruption is expected to intensify over the next two years. Credit markets are lagging equities in pricing disruption risk, with default rates forecast to rise by 1–4% across high yield, leveraged loans, and private credit. Redemption risk is concentrated in private BDCs, which represent about 22% of invested capital, and recent outflows are probably manageable on average. The locked up or permanent nature of most private credit capital means that sentiment shifts will likely impair new issuance volumes, and then trigger wider spreads. Historically, declines in loan issuance precede spread widening; we think this is coming. In 2026, leveraged loan issuance is down over 30% year-on-year, larger than what would be implied from spreads 35–40bps wider YTD. We expect sustained pressure on loan spreads in the coming months. Near-term catalysts—including Tuesday's Anthropic announcement and future AI model releases - could accelerate repricing. That said, we see significant opportunities for investors to differentiate winners and losers, particularly in credit markets. However, if "third country equivalence" would also allowed third country CB to become LCR level 1 eligible in the EU it would only be more generous than BIS recommendations also for third country CB (which recommends LCR level 2A), it would also be more generous than most third countries themselves (which typically do only allow LCR level 2A eligibility, if any). Section 301 of the Trade of Act of 1974 has withstood legal challenge and, after investigation and an implementation process, can be used to apply bilateral tariffs to address unfair trade practices. By doing so for the top ten trading partners, the administration could impose almost the same level of aggregate tariff in place prior to the Court ruling. Following that script, the USTR announced Section 301 investigations into the US's top trading partners following the ruling. The Friday proclamation imposing the 10% universal tariff included two annexes outlining exemptions from the 15% universal tariff, see here and here. We estimate that the exemptions are relatively similar to those already in place under the prior reciprocal tariff structure carving out goods already covered by sectoral tariffs, pharmaceuticals, and a number of products which the US does not domestically produce in large enough quantities. records.text: Mechanics of the LCR The US Agencies’ LCR is a metric that compares high quality liquid assets (HQLA) to how much its funding could flow out (net cash outflows), and for G-SIBs, must be greater than or equal to 100% (for a depiction of LCR, see Exhibit 12). Both HQLA and net cash outflows receive modifiers, based on the “quality” of the type of asset or funding source. Cash and low credit risk securities (i.e., UST and GNMA) receive maximum HQLA value, and deposits are included in net cash outflows, and depending on the type of deposit, they have different deposit outflow modifiers. Retail deposits are deemed sticky, or high “quality” and have a low modifier, whereas institutional deposits, especially non-operational deposits, have a high modifier. We note that the Fed’s quantitative easing results in material creation of non-operational deposits, as asset managers end up with cash after selling securities to the Fed that they then deposit at their custody bank (see our report from 2020 here). As a result, in a period of QE, banks with large custody businesses see greater pressure on LCRs from deposit growth than other banks, as more of their deposit growth is in the form of non-operational deposits that have low LCR value. records.text: 523/02/2026 Tech productivity growth accelerates: Total French productivity has started to recover. It has risen at a 1% y/y pace over the past three years, and was back to pre- Covid levels last year. In the information and communication (I&C) sector, which is most impacted by AI, productivity is now about 15% higher than in 2019 and the growth trajectory has been accelerating above the pre-Covid trend over the past three years (Figure 12). Although the I&C sector accounts for only around 6% of total value added, we estimate that its rising productivity contributed roughly 25% of the overall productivity pickup seen in the past three years. Future stronger activity in these sectors should thus prolong this positive traction in France productivity. Lower supply constraints: Post-Covid, French productivity was hampered by supply-chain constraints, including labour shortages. Even as activity fell, many firms chose to retain their workforce, thus having a negative impact on productivity. The easing of these constraints has now helped both activity and corporate flexibility, allowing firms to adjust staffing when needed (Figure 13). While GDP grew 0.9% y/y last year, employment fell by about 50k, further supporting the productivity gain. Labour shortages were especially acute in the ‘other transport’ sector (aeronautics and defence) during 2023-24, with the INSEE business survey showing a sharp rise in hiring difficulties (Figure 14). records.text: Giovanni Pierdomenico +44(20)7051-6807 | giovanni.pierdomenico@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Europe: Limited Implications From the Recent US Tariffs News for Europe 22 February 2026 | 10:59PM GMT BOTTOM LINE: On February 20th, the US Supreme Court struck down the tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), including the “reciprocal” tariffs that accounted for part of the increase in the US effective tariff rate on imports from Europe. Shortly after the Supreme Court ruling, President Trump announced a 10% “global tariff” under Sec. 122, with subsequent communication pointing to a further rise to 15%. The new “global tariff” is subject to very similar exemptions as the previous reciprocal tariff and would thus apply to around 50% of US imports from the EU and around 60% of imports from the UK. The replacement of IEEPA tariffs with a new 15% global tariff would raise the US effective tariff rate on the EU by 0.9pp to 12.1% and by 2.9pp to 10.9% for the UK but would be essentially neutral for Switzerland and Norway, although uncertainty remains elevated on a number of dimensions. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. records.text: headline GDP reflected noisy trade and inventories as well as a quirky, hard-to-estimate effect on the GDP deflator for federal government services due to the Q4 shutdown. This measurement issue is not relevant for forecasting the business cycle, the labor market or inflation. Looking for an H1 rebound: We see the Q4 GDP numbers as consistent with more AI-related capex to come. Underlying strength was evident in imports of products related to the AI capex buildout – computers, semiconductors and related equipment – but with less of a lift to related investment. We suspect this is a timing issue, and that the investment shows up over time. While AI investment looks strong, we note mild capex intentions in the non-AI corners of the economy. This echoes the ‘K-shaped’ US consumer theme, wherein a small slice of the sector accounts for most of the growth. We expect the government shutdown effect to reverse in Q1, adding back a percentage point to growth. Meanwhile, consumers should benefit in H1 from generous tax refunds, stimulative monetary policy and favorable financial conditions. KEY MESSAGES Higher-than-expected capex announcements from flagship technology companies factor into a lift to our forecasts for nonresidential investment as a component of US GDP. The net impact on GDP is lessened by surging imports, as was the case in the Q4 data. We also note that capex plans in non-AI sectors of the economy remain subdued. records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 28 Deutsche Bank AG Seasonality Framework: In this section, we examine the seasonality patterns across a range of rates products with a focus on EUR rates. We split the calendar year to 24 half- month periods for which we estimate a seasonal signal. The data we analyze are demeaned (to neutralize for periods of persistently rising or falling rates or spreads), while we also exclude extreme data points by looking at the trimmed mean (20%) adjusted for standard deviation (stronger signal for variables with smaller standard deviation). Among other things, we look at the median change and the hit ratio. The combination of all these metrics leads to a seasonality score that is reflected in the colour-coded heatmap in our table. To determine the strength of the signal, we also look at the success rate of the seasonal signal achieved over the five most recent years. For more details regarding our framework, please see the relevant publication. As per our read, the act provides the President the authority to impose temporary import measures – either an across-the-board import surcharge (tariffs) capped at 15% ad valorem, quotas, or both – when “fundamental international payments problems” require action. records.text: M Idea 2 Four Scenarios for the Oil Market Market signals: pricing risk premium repricing vs physical tightness The oil market sent a striking message this week: paper risk re-priced higher even as signals of physical tightness eased. Front-month flat price strengthened across all three benchmarks —Brent rose by around $3.1/bbl to ~$71.8/bbl, WTI by ~$3.5/bbl to ~$66.4/bbl, and Dubai by ~$3.7/bbl to ~$70.7/ bbl (week-on-week) - and freight indicators also moved higher. In options markets, Brent 3 month 25 delta risk reversals widened sharply, approaching the levels last observed during periods of acute uncertainty such as early 2022. Yet several measures that typically track prompt physical conditions moved in the opposite direction: the Brent M1–M2 spread narrowed (from roughly $0.7/bbl to ~$0.5/ bbl), Brent DFL declined materially (from about $0.9/bbl to ~$0.3/bbl), and Brent CFD compressed sharply (Week 1 from roughly $3.0/bbl to ~$0.7/bbl). Differentials for long- haul Atlantic Basin barrels also eased, including across West African and other arbitrage crudes - again, a pattern that is usually more consistent with loosening prompt supply than tightening. Taken together, the combination of higher flat prices, freight and risk-reversal skew alongside softer prompt spreads and weaker physical differentials reads as a classic signature of a market pricing geopolitical optionality and tail-risk hedging demand, rather than responding to immediate scarcity. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 effective tariff rate, as measured by US customs imports, remained subdued near ~10%. Nominal tariff levels were converging with effective levels; after the IEEPA ruling, we expect both to move lower. Replacing IEEPA with Section 122 tariffs of 15% and considering composition effects of US imports, we estimate baseline tariffs near 11%. Our estimate of "core" tariffs (ex fuels, gold and AI-related imports) remains closer to 13-14%. Were Section 122 tariffs not extended by Congress, the tariff level would fall to mid single digits, ~6-7%. The mid single digit range ex-Section 122 may be a lower bound for tariffs in the medium term. Thinking about a ceiling for tariffs, raising tariffs to levels comparable to the "risk" scenarios from around Liberation Day last year becomes quite complicated. Reliance on section-based tariffs and/or Congress will complicate the path to higher tariffs and reinforces our argument for a pivot from country to sector tariffs. FX: We see three key offsetting flow dynamics for the JPY currently.  Japanese investors have slowed buying of foreign assets this year, but signs of repatriation remain scarce.  Foreign investors have replaced domestic investors as the main source of super-long JGB inflows. This is a positive for the JPY to the extent that this equilibrium is maintained and flows are happening on an unhedged basis  Equity outflows by asset managers (likely reflecting NISA flows) have stepped up, as is typically the case in January. Policy credibility reflected by inflation convergence: Over the last few decades EM central banks have increasingly adopted official inflation-targeting regimes (see IMF link) and have managed to bring inflation expectations under control. Long-term CPI data shows a clear convergence between EM and DM (Figure 6). Even forward-looking indicators imply an outlook for tighter, less volatile inflation differentials (Figure 7). Tight inflation differentials also have a fundamental impact on FX via purchasing power parity. Large inflation differentials lead to nominal exchange rate depreciation in the long run (which is bad for fixed income returns) and the associated macro uncertainty contributes to higher FX volatility. We think the FX volatility convergence between EM and DM supports carry trades and improves the overall Sharpe ratio for the asset class compared to DM (Figure 8). This is not only the result of a weaker USD environment, it reflects policy credibility and macro uncertainty convergence, as we outline above. A few more factors contribute to vol compression, in our view: External vulnerability: Historically, one of the most important vulnerabilities for EM has been the reliance on FX debt, particularly on public balance sheets. This reliance resulted in the asset class’s highly cyclical behaviour (i.e. vol). Any drain on FX liquidity due to tighter global financial conditions puts strain on public finances and increases the sensitivity of debt levels to currency fluctuations. However, over the last two decades major EM economies have developed their local bond markets and public finances have relied more on local currency borrowing, reducing the underlying external vulnerability (Figure 9). RMB as an additional FX vol anchor: Trade and capital flow links between EM economies and China have risen over the years. The increased link in trade and capital flows between China and EM has increased the correlation of EM currencies to the RMB. records.text: US Economic Presentation23 February 2026 ab 14 Source: USATRADE, Haver, UBS calculations Trade: imports holding up, a big increase in tariffs Imports have been volatile, but the level isn’t all that dented despite a large hike in tariffs. The economy is likely yet to adjust to this tax hike. • Net exports shaved 4.7 pp off Q1 real GDP growth, then added 4.8 pp to Q2 GDP. Q3 real GDP was boosted 1.6pp. It's obscured what is unfolding in the economy. • One thing is clear. The sizeable decoupling of the US from global trade we though might unfold following the April 2 announcements has not transpired. While we expect imports to suffer from the tariffs in the coming few years, the looming adjustment looks pretty modest. • We estimate that the current set of tariff policies in place would imply a weighted-average tariff of 12.9% using 2024 import shares. That 12.9% rate we estimate is up from 2.5% at the turn of the year, and represents a 1.1% of GDP tax on imports. We estimate slippage to be roughly 1 pp, and our projection assumes a 11.9% effective tariff based on 2024 imports. • That baseline assumption for our projections represents a 10.4 pp increase or a roughly 1.0 pp of GDP tax. From that we estimate the 0.8 pp reduction in real GDP growth spread over four years but predominantly in 2025 and 2026. We are long a USDJPY call with topside European KO (FX: Positioning for a grind higher in USDJPY, dated 9 February) to express a long-USDJPY delta and short vol view over the next few months. Vol regime change: On page 1 we noted that FX vol correlations with US rates vol have fallen; in USDJPY the fall in correlation between spot and US rates spot (Figure 2) may be a more significant signal for a change in USDJPY behaviour. Typically-high correlation between USDJPY and US rates has led to muted volatility in the USDJPY forwards (higher US rates support spot but push forwards lower), but the realised volatility gap between USDJPY spot and USDJPY forwards has narrowed and is now almost zero in the 2y (Figure 3). This is similar to the dynamic seen during the Abenomics era of the early-2010s, and may signal a period of local dynamics supporting both USDJPY spot and USDJPY vol. records.text: ey Research forecasts. Perhaps the broadest market debate will come from Mexico and the USMCA negotiations. In contrast to South America, it appears that positioning is more neutral heading into this risk event. Most clients we speak to agree with our views regarding USMCA renegotiations leading to some updates, but without substantial, wholesale changes. It seems we and our clients are working with the assumption that Mexico will keep its relatively competitive position to supply the US economy with industrial goods. Yet, there are concerns about the path to get to final destination. In the event we end up with annual reviews, we suspect elevated uncertainty will keep dragging private investment and economic growth. Overall, the global renewed market appetite for EM assets has prevailed despite the usual pre-election concerns in Latin America. High real rates in Latin America, relative to other emerging markets, have supported inflows, and we see meaningful opportunity for a virtuous cycle with both fiscal and monetary policy. But timing of market expectations and economic realities are not always aligned. Because such a mismatch can lead to volatility, we suspect there will be opportunities because at the end of the day, we are constructive on the underlying economic backdrop.

We expect Fed pricing to remain relatively stable over the roll period. Repo outlook SOFR/FF basis (SERFF) pricing improved drastically since the Fed initiated reserve management purchases in December and amid seasonal bill paydowns. While bill issuance has turned positive, the Treasury’s cash balance is expected to decline with the start of tax refund season, which increases the supply of reserve balances. These two factors are expected to largely offset each other, keeping repo expectations relatively unchanged over the coming weeks. Positioning We analyze net positions held by asset managers and the “other reportables” category, which includes central banks, corporate treasuries, mortgage originators, and commercial banks. These investors are generally less price sensitive and tend to roll positions early to minimize delivery risk, which leads to technical price pressure on the calendar spreads. A stronger investment story: We have revised upward our forecast for France GDP growth this year to 1.3%, from 1.1% previously. The latest Q4 2025 GDP data show a long-awaited pickup in private consumption and housing investment. This creates a stronger carry-over into 2026 and less policy uncertainty, as the passing of the budget further reinforces a gradual recovery this year. This outlook has been part of our baseline scenario for several months. However, we think the case for an upside surprise in corporate investment has also strengthened. We now expect corporate investment to grow 1.9% y/y, versus the 1.1% we had forecast before and the modest 0.1% growth recorded last year. On the negative side, the political compromise needed to pass the budget has been reached through ongoing high taxation on corporates, especially the rolling over of the surtax on large corporates, which is expected to raise around EUR7.3bn again this year. Key Takeaways Headline tariffs peaked in late 2025; we estimate replacing IEEPA with Section 122 lowers headline tariffs from ~13% to 11%; without Section 122, tariffs would be ~6-7%. The path to higher tariffs is now more complicated, and the risk skew is to lower tariffs, reinforcing our view for lower US inflation in 2H26. Sector implications appear more consequential than macro implications given the size and scope of reconfigured tariffs. A year ago we argued sector tariffs would need to replace country tariffs because of legal foundations; the Supreme Court ruling could accelerate that process. records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General Channel surfing: There are three main channels for credit formation within the broader tech discussion: (1) public issuance, (2) bank lending and (3) private capital. Each one of these capital pools generally supports different business models, representative of the borrower’s lifecycle. We will broadly assume that the public debt markets are only accessible to the most mature issuers, although high yield is increasingly accessible to more marginal buyers. The traditional bank lending channels would typically provide capital to more downstream borrowers, although it is becoming more difficult to make generic bank lending statements with large banks showing a willingness to fund large lending pools to the AI leaders. Finally there is private capital, which we would broadly attribute as maintaining the riskier borrower profile. records.text: European Economic Perspectives23 February 2026 ab 9 To put this into the current context, over the past decade Eurozone productivity growth averaged only 0.5%, compared with 1.7% in the US. While this means that Europe could potentially more than double its productivity growth if it effectively adopts AI, given the size of the gap to the US, it appears unlikely that Europe will be able to catch up with the US. The IMF estimates suggest that higher-income countries are likely to experience higher productivity gains. This can be attributed to two factors: (1) higher-income countries tend to have a higher share of value added coming from AI-exposed sectors (e.g. financial services); and (2) higher wage levels (in higher-income countries) imply a higher potential for cost savings due to AI adoption. All in all, although Europe is clearly lagging the US in terms of investment and development of AI technologies and capabilities, it still has the potential to benefit as much as, or even more than, the US from AI-related productivity gains. However, to fully capture this potential, Europe needs to ensure effective adoption of AI. Historically, that scale of inventory absorption would likely require the front of the Brent curve to return to a mild contango later in the year. Applying our regression relationship to our projected stock trajectory suggests that, while a near-term de-escalation could pull Brent back toward the low-$60s, a later-year build in OECD commercial stocks could be consistent with a somewhat deeper contango and a front-month price nearer the high- $50s under purely fundamental conditions. In practice, however, prices are unlikely to be determined by pure fundamentals alone. Recent weeks have again highlighted that geopolitical risk premia can provide material support at the front end, particularly when prices soften, providing a negative feedback look when prices go lower. On this basis, our base-case expectation is for front-month Brent to drift toward ~$60/bbl as 2026 unfolds, but we see limited scope for sustained weakness materially below that level absent a clearer and more durable easing in geopolitical risk. records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. records.text: ab 23 February 2026 Global Research Canada Economic Perspectives IEEPA ruling - little immediate impact for Canada The SCOTUS ruling only impacts border tariffs The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) struck down tariffs which had been added using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). This includes the 35% tariff that was imposed on certain Canadian exports under the national emergency with respect to the border. Sectoral tariffs on steel, aluminum, copper, autos, among others, have been enacted under a different provision, section 232, and are therefore unaffected by the Supreme Court ruling last week. Ahead of the SCOTUS ruling we estimated that despite the high 35% tariff rate placed on Canadian exports under IEEPA increased compliance with the CUSMA (Canada-US- Mexico Agreement) had sheltered ~85% of Canadian exports from additional tariffs. With that we estimate that prior to the ruling the weighted average tariff rate (WATR) on Canadian exports to the US was ~3.6% with the bulk of this 2.9pp attributable to the sectoral tariffs not impacted the SCOTUS ruling. The US administration have announced the imposition of a universal 10% tariff, see the proclamation here, and the President over the weekend stated that this could potentially rise to 15%, see here. Note that the carve out for CUSMA compliance remains in place with this new policy. The WATR on Canadian exports would decline to 3.2% under a 10% regime or 3.3% under a 15% regime. This is a

records.text: 23 February 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG A look at the MoF's February 2026 Monthly Report In this update, we take a look at the February 2026 Monthly Report from the Federal Ministry of Finance (MoF) , which contains the first financial statistics data on federal budget developments in the new year. The analysis builds on our previous work regarding Germany's fiscal policy shift (see also here and here). It considers the latest dynamics of a) the federal government's core budget as well as b) the two major off-budgetary funds SV BW (Federal Armed Forces Fund) and SV IK (Infrastructure & Climate Protection Fund) for which the government provides monthly credit stock/flow data.1 Setting the stage: The finalized 2026 budget plan After the federal government's combined 2025 financing deficit for the core budget, the SV BW and the SV IK closed significantly lower than targeted by the government (c. EUR 110 bn or 2.5% of GDP vs. a planned EUR 143 bn or 3.2% of GDP) (see our analysis here), attention is now turning to 2026 for which the federal government plans an even higher credit-financed deficit. Our detailed analysis of Germany's fiscal outlook (up to and including 2029) can be found here. records.text: Based on our tariff and passthrough assumptions, we estimate that the further impact on consumer prices will be minor from here. The left side of Exhibit 3 shows that we estimate that tariff passthrough increased core PCE prices by about 0.7% through January (extrapolating from CPI data for January), similar to or a touch smaller than other estimates, and will raise prices by a further 0.1% in the remainder of 2026. The right side of Exhibit 3, however, shows that a large gap will persist in year-over-year terms through the middle of this year between the official inflation rate and our estimate of the rate excluding tariff effects. The reason that we do not expect a net disinflationary impact in the remainder of 2026 despite the small decline in the effective tariff rate is that we would not expect companies to lower prices in response to tariff reductions nearly as quickly as they increased them in response to tariff increases. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 25 February 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : Trading Tariff and Tech turnovers KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Tariff turnover. In the space of a few days, US tariffs introduced under the International Emerging Economic Power Act (IEEPA) were ruled illegal by the Supreme Court, only to be reinstated via executive order at 15% under Section 122 of the 1974 Trade Act. The policy churn recalls the period around “Liberation Day” in 2025, but the economic impact should be far smaller. While a handful of countries, including the UK, have secured lower bilateral rates, for most – particularly India, Thailand and Vietnam – a 15% tariff represents little change or even a reduction from IEEPA levels. Crucially, these measures are potentially temporary, capped at 150 days. Drawing on Alberto Cavallo’s work on tariffs (see this week’s Three Thoughts), this should limit any residual inflation pass‑through. As a result, while questions around policy execution echo last spring, the shock to risk appetite is materially weaker. The macro backdrop is different, as is asset‑manager sentiment toward the USD, which is far softer than a year ago. We therefore retain a modest USD short versus CAD, but do not extend our negative dollar stance. Tech turnover. The Tech sector is another notable source of changing market narrative and turnover. records.text: FX VALUATION 1924 February 2026 BNP Paribas STEER STEER is our Short-Term Equilibrium Exchange Rate trading model that estimates the fair value of G10 and EM currencies based on short- term market fundamentals. These include relative equities, relative rates, relative curve steepness, risk sentiment and credit risk. ▪ STEER provides a market-based fair value for FX. Deviations from fair value tend to last only 1-2 weeks, with the exchange rate more likely to move back toward its fair value. ▪ We compared the performance of STEER with more complex machine learning (ML) models and found that models like Least-angle Regression (Sharpe: 0.7) and Support Vector Regression (Sharpe: 0.74) perform broadly in line with STEER (Sharpe: 0.63) while the Random Forest model underperforms (Sharpe: 0.17). ▪ The ML models can have an edge during periods where factors decouple, like after Liberation Day or the 2023 cycle of rate-hiking. records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 78 Deutsche Bank AG IEEPA ruling: A risk for fiscal & inflation In its recent fiscal outlook, the CBO projects receipts from customs duties of USD418bn (1.3% of GDP) this year, assuming an average import tariff rate of ~15%. Actual revenue from import duties has however been lower than implied by statutory tariffs, with the most recent three-month run rate at ~USD28bn, or 336bn annualised (1.1% of GDP). Moreover, betting markets imply a ~75% probability of a Supreme Court ruling against IEEPA tariffs. The latter account for the majority of the import duties collected over the past year, with CBP data implying that ~60/70% of the FY25 & FY26 duties was collected under IEEPA authority (Figure 215). This suggests that without IEEPA, tariff revenue could be expected to be around 0.5% of GDP, at least if the revenue is not replaced by other tax/tariff measures or spending cuts--implying a positive fiscal impulse for this year. As far as the inflation impact is concerned, a possible removal of IEEPA tariffs would be significant in principle, not only because of their high share in overall duties, but also because, apart from section 232 auto tariffs, consumer goods tariffs are typically imposed under IEEPA and are hence more directly relevant for CPI inflation than remaining ‘sectoral’ tariffs.3 In practice, the assessment is complicated by the fact that a significant part of the price effects have already occurred. records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 80 Deutsche Bank AG An unsurprising breakdown Front-end US rates have recently diverged from economic data surprises after having tracked them relatively closely over the past few years (albeit with a lag at times), as shown in today’s chart. We see three factors at play. First, market participants anticipate a modestly dovish shift in Fed policy under new leadership, independent of the data. The effects of this can be seen in the persistent pricing of additional cuts at the June FOMC meeting, the first under Chair Powell’s successor, and in related SOFR butterflies. A survey of market views on Fed independence that we conducted last fall suggests the shifting composition of the Committee is expected to lead to a roughly 25bp lower fed funds rate than would otherwise be the case. Second, the government shutdown last year produced significant noise in official economic statistics and likely muted the market response to them. In line with this, a recent FICOTD showed that the yield impact of payrolls and CPI inflation surprises fell notably late last year. With the normalized data release calendar, some of the linkage to front-end rates may re-establish. And third, intensifying concerns around AI and potential non-linear impacts on employment have the market less tethered to backward-looking data that may prove more “stale” than usual. records.text: M Idea 4 Scenario 1 - No Supply Disruption: De-escalation and Risk Premium Unwind • Reference scenario; meaningful possibility • No impact on production or exports • Risk premium of $7-9 dissipated: Brent falls back to low/mid-$60s In this scenario, diplomatic pressure combined with visible US military positioning proves sufficient to induce a negotiated adjustment in Iran’s nuclear posture, avoiding direct military confrontation. Talks may remain protracted and incremental, but the threat of force serves primarily as leverage rather than as a precursor to kinetic action. Sanctions enforcement could remain firm, but no additional restrictions are imposed that materially alter current export flows. Under this outcome, physical oil supply remains broadly unchanged. Iranian exports continue at roughly recent levels, and regional transit through the Strait of Hormuz is unaffected. The primary market effect would be the removal of the geopolitical risk premium currently embedded in front-end prices. Based on our regression analysis of OECD commercial inventories against the Brent M1–M4 calendar spread over the past 25+ years (see accompanying chart), current stock levels would be consistent with a flat to slightly contangoed structure rather than the prevailing backwardation. records.text: Tariffs and the Economy After the Supreme Court Ruling On Feb. 20, the Supreme Court ruled against the tariffs the Trump Administration imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), in a 6-3 decision. This includes the “reciprocal” tariffs applied on trading partners at various rates as well as tariffs applied to Canada, China, Mexico and other countries under separate emergency declarations, but it does not affect tariffs imposed under other laws (e.g., the metals and auto tariffs imposed under Sec. 232, or the 2018-2019 China-focused tariffs under Sec. 301). The court’s decision is silent on the question of refunds, which is likely to lead importers to seek repayment in a separate process in lower courts. To date, we estimate IEEPA tariffs have collected around $180bn and we expect most of this to be refunded in increments over the next year or so. As expected, President Trump responded by announcing a new “global tariff” under Sec. 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to replace the prior reciprocal tariff regime. An executive order signed Feb. 20 imposed a 10% surcharge on imports from all countries, with essentially the same exemptions as the prior reciprocal tariffs (energy, precious metals, a number of other products subject to current or prospective Sec. 232 sectoral tariffs and USMCA-compliant imports from Canada and Mexico). records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 13 Step 1: Fleeting mechanical step down in tariffs An adverse ruling removes the IEEPA “scaffolding” – reciprocal tariffs, the 10% fentanyl baseline tariffs on China, 25% Secondary Russian Oil Tariffs on India, and 35% fentanyl tariffs on non-USMCA compliant imports from Mexico and Canada. This mechanically lowers the effective US tariff rate, with the largest near term relief in high tariff, non deal economies (India and a few others) where IEEPA currently delivers combined tariff rates of 30–50% (well above what any single alternative authority can replicate quickly under current law). In theory, were the administration to choose not to replace IEEPA tariffs for all partners, or if Section 122-based tariffs expire, the tariff rate could shift lower by ~5%-6%. Step 2: Short term bridge option via Section 122 To avoid a sudden collapse in negotiations, the tariff infrastructure pivots to Section 122 as a bridge authority. Section 122 can support across-the-board tariffs of up to 15% for 150 days, which is sufficient to restore an urgency to the dialogue. At a product-level, treatment remains unchanged – USMCA-compliant products continue to be exempted, along with the goods that were previously exempted from IEEPA-based tariffs. This includes goods that are currently facing either Section 232 based tariffs, or relevant investigations. We discuss how this affects tariffs at a country and sector level here. The market response would likely be concentrated at the front of the curve: prompt spreads would be expected to widen and remain supported for longer than in Scenario 2, reflecting a more persistent physical tightening. Saudi Arabia and the UAE would have scope to offset a significant portion of a 1+ mb/d shortfall, although the pace of any response—and market confidence in that response—would be critical for price dynamics. records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 13 Euroland Strategy EGBs Relative Value Corner This week has been the first week of 2026 without an EGB syndication by any of the 10 largest issuers. We still expect Spain to conduct its 2nd syndication (long-end of the curve) of the year in February, as it has been doing consistently over the past few years. The lack of syndications coincided with a notable drop in term premia, with our 5s10s TP proxy down 4bp from its peak earlier in February. The combined front- end rally and lower term premia drove the Bund yield lower, by almost 15bp from its February peak. Nonetheless, this move wasn’t EUR rates specific as both 10y UST & UKT outperformed vs the Bund within this timeframe. In the 1970s context – still close to Bretton Woods – a “payments problem” had a concrete meaning tied to reserve loss and forced adjustment under fixed exchange rates. In today’s U.S. regime (floating FX, monetary sovereignty, liabilities largely in domestic currency), we would not view a persistent trade deficit as constituting a classic balance of payments “crisis” or solvency constraint. That said, a disorderly dollar depreciation driven by a reversal in capital inflows (and associated asset price weakness) is a conceivable pathway to the type of broader external disequilibrium contemplated by the statute. We find good reason to think that near-term tariffs are capped below Liberation Day levels – at least until Section 232 and 301 investigations are complete – for several reasons. First, Section 122 specifies a 15% cap. Second, its authority is temporary without Congressional reauthorization. And third, the fact that the authority has never been used and references balance of payments disequilibrium and not trade deficits may leave it open to legal challenges. We discuss the details below in Tariffs in Theory and Practice.

Applied to Hormuz-origin flows, this implies a reduction of close to 2 billion tonne-miles per day in effective transport capacity, equivalent to around 6% of global crude shipping capacity. Given current seaborne crude flows of roughly 50 mb/d, this would correspond to an effective tightening on the order of 2–3 mb/d for a period of several weeks. While shipping markets would adapt over time through higher freight rates, reallocation of tonnage, and operational adjustments, the initial effect could be significant relative to available spare capacity. From a balance perspective, such a disruption would likely exceed the offset that could be achieved through a pause in Chinese discretionary stockbuilding alone and would test the practical limits of Saudi and UAE spare capacity. In this respect, the price and curve response could begin to resemble early-2022 dynamics, when the market questioned whether available buffers were sufficient to absorb a multi million barrel per day shortfall and repriced the front of the curve accordingly. The market response would likely be concentrated at the front of the curve, with Brent moving sharply higher and prompt spreads widening materially as refiners and traders compete for near-term barrels. In its recent fiscal outlook, the CBO projects receipts from customs duties of USD418bn (1.3% of GDP) this year, assuming an average import tariff rate of ~15%. Actual revenue from import duties has however been lower than implied by statutory tariffs, with the most recent three -month run rate at ~USD 28bn, or 336bn annualised (1.1% of GDP). Moreover, betting markets imply a ~75% probability of a Supreme Court ruling against IEEPA tariffs. The latter account for the majority of the import duties collected over the past year, with CBP data implying that ~60/70% of the FY25 & FY26 duties was collected under IEEPA authority ( Figure 6). From the standpoint of our baseline outlook for the US economy, the move to lower net tariffs reinforces our view for lower inflation in the second half of the year. Lower tariffs were anticipated in our forecasts and, in isolation, are unlikely to materially alter the expected path of economic activity relative to our baseline through 2Q26. For now, Section 122 tariffs represent the new legal basis to hold tariffs at a similar level. The tariff levels we have estimated above are also in line with the tariff rate implied by CBO's assumptions around the customs duties for 2026 and 2027. Further, refunds are quantitatively limited (we assume $85bn, corresponding to the midpoint of our estimated range of outcomes), and, given the lack of clarity by the Supreme Court, refunds are likely to take a while to reach the economy. Were Section 122 to expire at the end of the 150 days, and not be renewed, then tariff rates would move materially lower in 3Q26. There may be a further uplift to domestic demand, and we may move closer to our upside demand scenario. Any incremental uplifts to the corporate margins and additional goods disinflation would be further supportive of labor demand and household spending. As we note above, in our view, perhaps the most important outcome of the Supreme Court's ruling on IEEPA tariffs is that there is a near-term ceiling for how high the effective tariff rate can go. Sector-Level Implications As country-level differences go away, in the near term, product-level tariffs should fall into two buckets – convergence to 15% tariffs (plus existing MFN/ Section 301 tariffs), or Section 232 rates. Under IEEPA, the composition of imports interacting with a range of economy-level tariffs resulted in a large range for product-level tariffs. Replacing IEEPA-based tariffs with broad- based 15% tariffs reduces the dispersion in product-level tariffs. At a sector level, consumer sectors see the greatest relief. In our note on Consumer goods-related IEEPA tariffs, we expected the IEEPA ruling to benefit consumer categories; however, with tariff levels being raised to 15% from 10%, as we had previously expected, the boost is likely to be smaller. Given that Section 122 has less legal precedent than IEEPA – Section 122 has never been used – we think it is useful to revisit the law and its interpretation, with the understanding that we are economists and not trade lawyers. According to our reading, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 gives the President the authority to impose temporary import restrictions, including tariffs or quotas, when certain international payment problems exist. If triggered, the President may impose tariffs of up to 15% for 150 days, with any extension subject to congressional approval. Unlike Section 232 or 301, no formal investigation is required to make the determination. Specifically, Section 122(a) says, “Whenever fundamental international payments problems require special import measures to restrict imports – (1) to deal with large and serious United States balance-of-payments deficits, (2) to prevent an imminent and significant depreciation of the dollar in foreign exchange markets, or (3) to cooperate with other countries in correcting an international balance-of-payments disequilibrium (emphasis added), the President shall proclaim, for a period not exceeding 150 days (unless such period is extended by Act of Congress) – (A) a temporary import surcharge, not to exceed 15 percent ad valorem, in the form of duties (in addition to those already imposed, if any) on articles imported into the United States; (B) temporary limitations
