records.text: ome cases, capital controls. A "balance of payments crisis" was effectively defined as reserve depletion under a pegged exchange rate. After the collapse of the Bretton Woods system, the US shifted to a floating exchange rate, where the dollar adjusts endogenously to shifts in capital and current account dynamics. The Fed is not defending a gold peg and the US does not have a binding reserve constraint in the same way as it did (around the time when the Trade Act of 1974 was written). In our view, a balance of payments crisis is not applicable for the US given its floating exchange rate, monetary sovereignty, and government debt denominated in its own currency. A persistent trade deficit alone cannot create a solvency constraint. That said, it is possible for the US to experience general disequilibria through a sharp depreciation in the dollar and asset prices if, for example, foreign demand for US dollar assets fell and prior capital inflows turned to capital outflows. If persistent, this would cause a deterioration in the net international investment position, pushing risk premia higher, weakening the dollar, and potentially creating upward pressure on import prices. Again, we are not trade lawyers, but we find good reason to think that near-term tariffs are capped – and capped below Liberation Day levels – at least until Section 232 and 301 investigations are complete for several reasons. Determining eligibility and procedures for refunds now falls to the Court of International Trade, complicating matters as hundreds of tariff refund lawsuits are pending. Justice Kavanaugh described the issue of refunds as “a mess.” Meanwhile, tariffs continue to have an outsized impact on goods prices; both imported goods affected by tariffs and domestic goods driven by retailers looking to pass costs along (Figure 1). Although Trump is expected to quickly implement his backup plan, rebates and a narrower range of tariffs could help reduce price pressures, which is positive news. On the downside, many investors and economists (including the CBO) have already included tariffs in their forecasts. Without tariffs, the US deficit as a percentage of GDP appears more strained (Figure 2). A less favourable fiscal outlook than previously anticipated, coupled with the possibility of moderated goods prices, is likely to exert downward pressure on the US dollar (see Figure 3). records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 81 EGB spreads start 2026 with last year's momentum In today’s FICOTD we take a first look at the relative YTD performance of EGB spreads vs other risky assets as well as among individual countries. To do that we’ll deploy our regular risky assets PCA (principal component analysis) with some modifications. We start by performing a PCA on risky assets such as VIX, DAX, SX5E, iTraxx Main & Crossover, i.e. a combination of volatility, equity and credit spread indices, with a sample period since the start of 2025. We then isolate PC1 (first principal component) which explains 80% of the cross variation of these risky assets. This should capture the risk on/off appetite in markets. Next, we regress each 10yr EGB spread (vs Bund) vs this PC1 using the entire 2025 period as our sample. This leads to obtaining a beta for each EGB spread, with BTP/ Bund having the highest and DSL/Bund the lowest as would be expected. Finally, we treat the 2026 YTD period as out of sample, and we estimate the over or under performance of each 10yr EGB spread beta hedged vs PC1. We present the evolution of the YTD cumulative residuals across countries. The first takeaway is that all EGB spreads have a negative YTD residual, i.e. they have outperformed vs other risky assets, with the average EGB spreads’ residual at around -3bp. records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Bond Market Strategy The (AI) tail wags the (fiscal) dog The recent price action is best interpreted as the market assigning an increased probability of a significant rise in unemployment due to automation. The past 5,000 years represent a long history of technological progress, during which neither has unemployment risen relentlessly nor has inflation declined relentlessly. However, there are plausible arguments that this time is somewhat different, in that the scale of AI and its pace of adoption may prove disruptive to the labour market, at least in the short term. Moreover, the uncertainty about the impact of AI may in itself generate a demand pullback. However, what is unlikely to be different is that in a world of fiat money, long-term inflation depends on policy choices. After all, Friedman did not say that inflation is always and everywhere a technological phenomenon. For a lasting deflationary impact, two conditions would need to be true: (1) AI is more of a substitute for than a complement to labour; and (2) there is no policy response to compensate for its impact. While the former is possible in the short run, the latter seems unlikely. In the current political environment, one should expect significant fiscal support for unemployment on top of the already long list of desired fiscal spending: energy independence, critical minerals, AI investments, defence, and support for an ageing population. STEER indicates that in Latam, USDCOP appears around 1 z-score rich as the pair’s spot has started to overshoot the recent rise in fair value due to higher oil prices and a widening of the local CDS (Figure 1). While the dislocation is smaller than the 1.5 z-score threshold to trigger a trade, our CTA projections favour adding short exposure to the pair, as CTAs are likely to keep building longs on the COP even if the spot remains unchanged, while they are likely to remain entrenched even if the COP declines, according to our analysis (Figure 2). This we think indicates that a possible decline in spot is likely to overshoot the current fair value. We therefore enter a short USDCOP position, targeting the pair’s fair value band of 3622.49

The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

An unofficial assessment of the fiscal rules: Though there will not be an official assessment, backing out the “headroom” against the fiscal rules is not exactly difficult. Given the recent favourable move in gilt yields, the lack of further policy announcements and the buffer built into the Autumn Budget, we expect the OBR’s projections to confirm indirectly that the government remains compliant with both of its fiscal rules: ▪ Deficit rule: The current budget balance should be in surplus by 2029/30, or the third year of the forecast horizon. ▪ Debt rule: Public sector net financial liabilities should be declining as a share of GDP in 2029–30, or the third year of the forecast horizon. We expect pre-policy headroom against the deficit rule to be GBP20bn and GBP23bn against the debt rule, relative to GBP22bn in November’s budget. This will break the pattern established by the last three fiscal events, limiting uncertainty for consumers and firms – at least for now. The key challenge to these views near term stem s from geopolitical escalation, particularly kinetic action against Iran. Comments that ‘good progress’ was made in the second round of US-Iran talks in Geneva last Tuesday (18 Feb) initially pushed crude prices down. However, this proved short-lived as the market quickly refocused its attention on the continued movement of US military assets into the region, with Brent crude above USD70/bbl going into the weekend. In terms of the actual talks, it is worth flagging that the respective negotiating positions are still wide apart and a date for the next round of talks has yet to be set. Friday’s news was dominated by a 15-day deadline for Iran to come to a deal on its nuclear programme, potentially reducing the likelihood of imminent military action. We estimate the market is pricing in about a USD10/bbl premium into the oil price, which we consider reasonable. Military action could occur at any moment and we do not have high conviction on exactly when. However, our view is that such action becomes more likely as crude prices come down . records.text: 323/02/2026 French investment benefiting from the shift to AI: The second half of 2025 saw corporate investment emerge from recession, rising 1.1% year-on-year in Q4, reflecting a weaker drag from goods-related and construction investment and, as in other advanced economies, a contribution from the AI-investment trend. Given the latest business-survey results and foreign direct investment data, we expect this positive impact to strengthen further. Over the past decade, service investment in Information and Communication (I&C) has been more buoyant than other types of investment, and the post-Covid period added extra momentum. In 2025, I&C investment grew around 3-4% y/y and now represents roughly 25% of total corporate investment, up from 15% in 2014. We estimate it has contributed about 0.1 percentage points to GDP growth in the past three years, though the net effect may be slightly lower because of a larger import component (Figure 6). Survey points further north: While investment to extend capacity has been declining somewhat in recent years, INSEE surveys show a greater willingness among businesses to invest to upgrade capacity, reflecting a shift toward higher-value IT services (Figure 7). records.text: Scenario 3: We see up to a 29pp uplift to LCRs from including a portion of Fed discount window capacity in LCR The existing LCR framework does not allow banks to include credit for available discount window capacity from pre-pledged collateral at their Federal Reserve bank. If a portion of the outstanding capacity could be included within the LCR calculation as an offsetting cash inflow, we see up to a 20% reduction in adjusted NCOs across the banks, which would result in LCR ratios rising by up to 29pp. As discussed in industry publications (see here), we believe available pre-pledged Fed discount window capacity, would be considered a cash inflow within the net cash outflow calculation. This funding would reduce adjusted net cash outflows in the denominator of the LCR calculation (Exhibit 12). Within our coverage, only PNC discloses the breakdown between available FHLB capacity and Fed capacity, whereas others report a combined Fed discount window + FHLB capacity. We therefore apply the PNC split (Fed discount window capacity comprised ~60% of the total combined available capacity) to the remaining banks’ Fed discount window borrowing capacity. Since banks rarely utilize the full limit, due to the potential market stigma from tapping the window, we assume only 50% of banks’ available capacity at the discount window is counted as a cash inflow in LCR. This observation summarises the basic textbook interpretation of technological progress (with some additional theory to back it up). One example of such an interpretation is Jason Furman’s recent FT op-ed. He argued that higher productivity from AI should increase real rates, as there is more investment (capex for AI) and less saving (due to the expectation of higher income from increased workers' productivity). The inflation impact is ambiguous, as higher spending in anticipation of higher future income may offset the productivity gains. Similarly, when we asked AI about its impact on rates, it also cautiously sided with historical precedents and the textbook conclusion, pointing towards higher rates. Is this time different? More specifically, will AI prove to be more of a substitute for than a complement to the labour market and result in lower, rather than higher, expected wages, thereby depressing demand? There is a plausible argument that the scale of AI and its speed of adoption increase the odds that it will be a substitute for labour, at least in the short term. Moreover, the labour market will most likely lag financial markets if there are risks of a significant disruption. This tempers the comfort one takes from resilient data. If the front of the curve were to move into contango while longer-dated Brent prices remained broadly anchored, this would imply front-month Brent in the low-to-mid $60s per barrel, compared with current levels around the low $70s. This suggests that roughly $7–9 per barrel of geopolitical premium could unwind relatively quickly in a de-escalation scenario. The majority of the adjustment would likely occur within days to weeks rather than months, particularly if market participants gain confidence that regional supply and transit flows will remain uninterrupted. A recent precedent illustrates the speed with which such premia can unwind. In June 2025, following the Iran-Israel war, Brent rallied sharply from the mid-$60s to close to $80/bbl on fears of broader regional escalation and potential disruption to Gulf exports. However, as it became evident that energy infrastructure and transit flows were not materially affected, prices retraced within weeks back toward pre strike levels. The episode underscores that when physical supply remains intact, geopolitical premia can both build and dissipate rapidly. Volatility would likely compress and the front of the curve could shift into contango as physical balances, rather than geopolitical risk

records.text: uggesting a long-delta bias may be favourable. With low implied vol, USDCNH spot also screens as a high carry/vol currency pair. While this structure has a very small directional delta exposure , we think adding a positive carry bias – supported by the positive delta signals elsewhere – helps the short-vol nature of this trade idea. Short vol in a limited-loss format: The characteristics of USDCNH spot and vol behaviour are similar to pegged currencies: very low realised vol with day-to-day moves strongly influenced by fixings. For a fully pegged currency, vol pricing may be discontinuous: at-the- money vol may trend lower as stable day-to-day FX levels mean realised vol is extremely low. However, a change in the peg regime may be under -priced due to this extremely low anchor . In the case of US DCNH, we think this suggests that selling call vol in a limited -loss format is prudent. We add a call fly with strikes set such that current USDCNH spot is in -the-money. This structure has a positive decay profile , and while it loses positive delta if spot rises above 7.00 in the short -term, the maximum loss is equal to the premium spent. All else equal , the structure earns elevated risk premium from selling topside vol with the high strikes decay more quickly than the near -the-money option, earning premium over the life of the structure. In the best case where USDCNH spot is 6.95 in six months , this structure would be worth seven-times its initial premium. Oliver Brennan, FX

records.text: on 0.22 Durbin-Watson stat 1.95 Source: J.P. Morgan calculations The first is the employment nowcast. Stronger employment implies lower unemployment, all else equal. A 1%-pt acceler- ation in employment growth would be expected to prompt an additional 0.1% reduction in the unemployment over the fol- lowing three months (and 0.4% if sustained for a year). Secondly, the model exploits time series patterns in past data to help predict the future. If households interviewed in the prior two months have reported increases in their unemploy- ment rates since they were last questioned (i.e. three months earlier) then the group of households interviewed the follow- ing month is statistically more likely to report a similar change. A percentage point increase in the unemployment rate reported by households in the prior two monthly samples would be expected to lead to an additional 0.2%-pt increase next sample. This influence is relatively small, however. Third, the model exploits the tendency for single-month unemployment rates to converge towards their neighbouring months when there are outliers. For example, if the prior three months showed single month unemployment rates of 6%, 5% and 5%, respectively, the 6% reported by the first group of households would be expected to converge towards 5% the next time it is sampled. Each 1%-pt deviation from the rest of the pack would be expected to produce a 0.5%-pt correction the next time this grouping is sampled. On a trajectory to 5.5% by 2Q

Our view of mildly higher rates is primarily predicated on structurally easier fiscal policy globally, tempered by two tail risks from AI (either a bubble or a significant threat to employment). Our mildly bearish duration bias has been challenged in recent days. This is unlikely to be justified by the latest data, which, if anything, has indicated a mild improvement in the labour market. Rather, the recent price action is best interpreted as the market assigning an increased probability that one of the aforementioned AI tails—a significant rise in unemployment due to automation— will materialise in the future. Historically, technological progress has generated disruptions to the labour market but no persistent, long-term upward trends in unemployment. Moreover, Friedman quipped that “inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon” (or, more precisely, a joint monetary and fiscal phenomenon) rather than “inflation is always and everywhere the result of technological progress”. records.text: On the flashing yellow lane is the increase in the default profile of PE firms, even relative to an overall increase in market default dynamics. As shown in Figure 4, default risk is generally rising across the market but remains within the range of recent historical experience. By contrast, Figure 7 highlights rising credit event risk across the private credit complex, although the more aggressive rise in Blue Owl’s default risk simply brings it to the industry average. For sure these business models have become more aggressive as demand for capital has grown. This growth has nonetheless not come at the expense of excessive leverage (one of the best measurements of private capital solvency in our view), with practically all large credit providers showing improving net debt/EBITDA ratios since the depths of the pandemic (Figure 8). The improvements are most notable outside of Blue Owl, which partially explains a closing of the default profile gap across the industry. China: Limited economic impact with US-China tariffs to persist US-China tariffs to persist: As China faces the highest tariff rates at the outset, it should also see the largest tariff reduction, which we estimate at around 7pp on a trade weighted basis. We believe this tariff reduction, at least temporarily, could lead to front loading of imports from China. However, after the 150 day period for Section 122 tariffs, the US government is likely to pursue more durable measures through Section 301 – addressing unfair trade practices – and Section 232 – citing national security concerns.Our China economics team notes that multiple Section 301 investigations are already underway involving China, covering areas such as the Phase 1 deal, maritime and shipbuilding, and semiconductors, with scope for additional inquiries. These developments, particularly in light of President Trump’s upcoming visit to China, reinforce our view that the US-China trade truce remains fragile. As a baseline, we expect bilateral tariff levels to persist, although the sectoral composition may shift over time. Limited economic impact in baseline scenario: Our China economics team highlights that direct trade between the US and China has already sharply declined, with US-bound shipments now representing only 11% of China’s total exports (down from 19% before 2018), and imports from the US accounting for just 4% (previously 8%). Each dimension is then computed averaging a rich set of subindicators. The EU is the first, and essentially the only, major region with a comprehensive legally binding AI regulatory framework. While adopted to manage AI-related risks, the framework might well have the (unintended) consequence of slowing down AI adoption. The key pillar of the EU's AI regulatory framework is the EU AI Act, which sets out rules for specific AI uses, for AI developers and deployers, dependent on the level of risk. The AI Act puts in place transparency and copyright-related rules for providers of AI models. It came into force on 1 August 2024, with the application to be phased in over the course of 2026 and 2027 (although some delays are already taking place). In addition to the EU AI Act, Misch et al. (2025) outline two additional types of regulation in Europe: occupation-related regulations (licensing and training requirements for specific occupations) and data privacy laws. The ONS uses a rotating sample of 50,000 households per quarter, although only a third of the sample is included in any individual month. As such, the movement in the single-month unemployment rate from the month to the next is often mostly driven by sampling differ- ences rather than economic developments. However, this can be addressed by focussing on the change in the single month unemployment rate from three months ago. On this basis, 80% of the households interviewed in those two months will be the same. The model of the three-month change can explain around half of the movements in the single-month unemployment rate using just three pieces of information (Table 1). One might have assumed that a wobble in the US‑centric tech narrative and turbulence in the implementation of tariff policy could have created a Liberation Day‑like reassessment of risk appetite, and of US assets more specifically. But surprisingly little seems to have changed so far. In terms of the knee‑jerk price reaction, moves have been relatively modest, and the rally in Treasurie s, given the potential disruption to tariff revenue , is especially impressive and potentially important. For much of the past year, our data have shown a clear tilt in non‑US investor behaviour: consistently below‑par demand for Treasuries, relatively persistent forward sales of the USD (effectively hedging US asset exposures), and fairly continuous demand for US equities. The latter, perhaps surprisingly, has accelerated rather than decelerated in the past month—consistent with the idea that we are seeing a very specific rotation out of software, but not necessarily out of tech and US equities more broadly. Meanwhile, the recent performance of Treasuries in the face of policy disruption is encouraging. It suggests that fiscal concerns, for now, have been put on the back burner, although a sterner test will be whether this continues once equity markets stabilise USD sentiment. records.text: CROSS-ASSET MODELS 1524 February 2026 We extract and use the three most statistically important systemic drivers (principal components) of the x-asset portfolio in two sub- processes: ▪ MarFA Valuations: Fair values represent where an asset should be trading, based on past correlation and market trends. Deviations beyond permissible errors are considered significant and temporary. This enables the model to be forward-looking. ▪ di-MarFA : Driver identification of MarFA is where we seek to find drivers behind principal components, to understand and isolate the macro variables that are key for broad market prices. BNP Paribas MarFA BNP Paribas Market Factor Analysis (MarFA ) is our cross- asset model for identifying correlations between assets and the main market and macroeconomic factors currently driving them. The MarFA framework monitors the relationships between more than 400 assets across equity, rates, credit, FX and commodities using principal component analysis (PCA). ▪ MarFA Trading: A short-term model capturing relationships over a three-month horizon; idiosyncrasies and mispricing in the market are more easily captured, generating signals frequently. Deviations from MarFA Trading fair value (i.e. +/- 2 standard deviations) tend to last 1-2 weeks. ▪ MarFA Macro: A medium-term model capturing relationships over a one-year horizon that extracts short-term ‘macro’ themes and idiosyncrasies and mispricing driven by macroeconomics. The overall impact is calculated as a product of three parameters: AI exposure, AI adoption, and savings in terms of labour costs. According to Acemoglu (2024), the US AI exposure coefficient is 19.9%, meaning AI has the capability to perform c.20% of tasks, while the AI adoption rate is assumed to be 23%, reflecting the share of AI-exposed tasks where benefits exceed costs (meaning in 77% of the cases, the adoption of AI would not actually be profitability-enhancing). As regards labour costs, using an average of the three productivity estimates, Acemoglu (2024) calculates that the AI-driven labour cost reductions lead to a 15% total cost decline. Using Acemoglu's approach, the IMF estimates that, in Europe, AI could boost productivity by 0.8% over the course of five years (the authors define medium term as 5 years, versus 10 years by Acemoglu). (4) The expected impact is slightly higher than in the US, largely due to higher potential for cost savings (23% in Europe versus 15% in the US), while the AI adoption rate in Europe is estimated at 18% and the AI exposure coefficient at 19.9%. However, this analysis assumes that AI adoption rates are the same across countries and sectors within Europe. Soon after, President Trump announced that he was raising the 10% surcharge to 15%, but as of this writing the White House has not released additional detail or a new executive order. Tariffs under Sec. 122 are limited under law to 15%, which creates some near-term certainty as tariff rates cannot rise further without taking more administratively involved steps under other laws like Sec. 301. However, using Sec. 122 creates new uncertainty in two ways. First, it is not yet clear how trading partners with reciprocal tariffs under 15% would be treated, but we assume that this will mean an increase in the tariff rate, at least in the short run. Australia, Singapore, the UK, GCC countries, and many smaller economies faced a 10% reciprocal tariff rate prior to the court ruling, and this will rise to 15% if applied as an across-the-board surcharge, as seems likely. A few larger economies, notably the EU, Japan, Switzerland, and Taiwan, agreed to deals with the Trump administration that imposed a maximum 15% rate inclusive of the existing US tariff, which generally ranged between 0 and 2.5%. These trading partners look likely to face an incremental tariff increase assuming the 15% now “stacks” on top of the existing US tariff rate. Second, Sec. 122 limits these tariffs to 150 days “unless such period is extended by an act of Congress.” The Feb. 20 executive order specifies that the current rate expires July 24

records.text: 23 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 77 Swap spreads: Closer to fair value, but not there yet We stay tactically neutral on swap spreads. In our valuation model, spreads have recently moved closer to fair value, though they remain 3-5 bps too wide across the board. For 10y spreads, a regression against the 3m SOFR/FF basis, Fed UST holdings in the 5-10y sector, 1m10y implied vol, and the 10y term premium suggests a fair value of -47 bps (vs -42 bps current). Importantly, expectations for regulatory changes are not incorporated into our model. Investor sentiment and positions are also hard to estimate accurately, and they could move spread pricing in the near term. Our view for an aggressive deregulatory push and more freed-up bank capital may ultimately justify a higher fair value for spreads over the long term. Our intuition for linking spreads and regulation is that at the long end, spreads are tied to the economics of dealers holding Treasuries on balance sheet, with their excess yield over SOFR reflecting the cost of regulatory capital. Assuming a 4.5% capital charge and 12% target ROE, an economically breakeven spread is approximately -55 bps. Market conditions that affect the ability to earn this spread, such as balance sheet availability and volatility, are also reflected in the pricing. As a reminder, Waller has skewed dovish in his views, dissenting in favor of a 25bps rate cut at the January FOMC meeting, as he remained focused on downside risks to the labor market. However, there is potential for him to sound somewhat more hawkish this week, following the January jobs report, which lent further evidence of stabilization, and the hot December core PCE print, which lifted the year-over-year rate to 3.0%, exactly where it was a year prior. As a reminder, recent Fedspeak has on balance skewed hawkish. For example, Governor Miran last week noted that the recent strength in core goods inflation and more solid labor market data caused him to revise his view of appropriate policy this year. He now anticipates 100bps of cuts instead of 150bps. In addition, the minutes to the January FOMC meeting had three hawkish elements. This is also due to the fact that the total defense spending target for this year has been significantly increased again to about EUR 119 bn ( see Figure 7 and Figure 13). There were contrary developments in January: While the outflow of funds from the SV BW were low (consistent with the typical seasonality at the start of the year), core budget defense spending rose visibly in a yoy perspective (see Figure 8). There, defense expenditures were 48% higher compared to a year ago. Among these, expenditures for military procurement climbed by almost 46% (see Figure 13 and Figure 15). All in all, total defense expenditures, at about EUR 8 bn in January, climbed substantially above the previous year's value of c. EUR 5.6 bn. Nevertheless, the January spending was below the average monthly value of nearly EUR 10 bn that is numerically required for achieving the full-year target of about EUR 119 bn (see Figure 8). In today’s FICOTD we take a first look at the relative YTD performance of EGB spreads vs other risky assets as well as among individual countries. To do that we’ll deploy our regular risky assets PCA (principal component analysis) with some modifications. We start by performing a PCA on risky assets such as VIX, DAX, SX5E, iTraxx Main & Crossover, i.e. a combination of volatility, equity and credit spread indices, with a sample period since the start of 2025. We then isolate PC1 (first principal component) which explains 80% of the cross variation of these risky assets. This should capture the risk on/off appetite in markets. Next, we regress each 10yr EGB spread (vs Bund) vs this PC1 using the entire 2025 period as our sample. This leads to obtaining a beta for each EGB spread, with BTP/Bund having the highest and DSL/Bund the lowest as would be expected. Finally, we treat the 2026 YTD period as out of sample, and we estimate the over or under performance of each 10yr EGB spread beta hedged vs PC1. We present the evolution of the YTD cumulative residuals across countries. The first takeaway is that all EGB spreads have a negative YTD residual, i.e. they have outperformed vs other risky assets, with the average EGB spreads’ residual at around -3

records.text: ab 23 February 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives AI in Europe: Progress, opportunities and constraints Europe is behind on AI, but opportunities from AI adoption are still large With US GDP growth currently to a large extent driven by the boom in AI-related tech investment, a question we often get is how important artificial intelligence (AI) is for the Eurozone growth outlook. To answer this question, we have constructed an EU-wide dataset, based on a framework developed by the OECD to measure AI investment, which includes core technology as well as complementary (intangible) assets, such as skills and data. Our analysis shows that Europe is clearly lagging the US in terms of investment and development of AI technologies and capabilities, implying limited near- term impact on growth. However, Europe still has the potential to benefit as much as, or potentially even more than, the US from AI-related productivity gains. However, to fully capture this potential, Europe needs to ensure effective adoption of AI, which is likely to face obstacles, not least from regulation. Europe is lagging the US in AI investment Using the OECD measurement approach, we calculate that EU investment in AI amounted to €337bn or 1.9% of GDP in 2024 (Eurozone: €278bn or 1.8% of GDP). At the subcategory level, skills accounted for 55% of total AI investment, followed by data and equipment (29%), R&D (9%) and other intellectual property (7%). By contrast, policy-reserve-matched bonds that might be sold before maturity remain subject to scrutiny because the likelihood of recovery before a sale is unclear. Some insurers have already declared that they will retain under-par policy-reserve-match bonds until maturity in order to avoid impairment. Recent discussions about a possible revision of the accounting rules would allow such bonds to be treated like HTM securities once they fall below 50% of book value, i.e. they would not be automatically impaired based on market price. If that revision is adopted, the need for those hold-to- maturity declarations could disappear. In any case, even if a policy-reserve bond falls below the 50% threshold, an impairment does not automatically trigger a forced sale, and a change in accounting standards would not, by itself, cause insurers to radically alter their bond-selling behaviour. That said, a number of large insurers have already trimmed their policy-reserve-matched bond positions, apparently selling off securities that have become low- yielding and deeply under-par. Whether the accounting rules change or not, it is rational to dispose of low-coupon bonds that have suffered a 50% loss and redeploy the proceeds into more attractive opportunities, provided the insurer has sufficient capital flexibility. records.text: 2026: Same Surplus, More Bullish Stocks Composition We raise our 2026 Brent/WTI forecasts on lower OECD commercial stocks, which tend to matter more for prices than other stocks, (Exhibit 4) despite an unrevised 2.3mb/d 2026 surplus. For sure this type of thinking has hit the software sector particularly hard, as t his sub -group now lags the broader market by over 20 percentage points. Our challenge in embracing this narrative is that, quite frankly, no one knows where this will end up and to make investment decisions based on this futurist view is a guess on a long-term terminal value that is especially opaque. records.text: E M – L O CA L E YE S F O R A G L O B A L V IEW 325/02/2026 Figure 5 shows the asset composition of public-pension funds – including the Government Pension Investment Fund and the three mutual aid associations – as at the end of December 2025. Asset allocation follows the ‘benchmark portfolio’ model, with 25% allocated to each category. Although JGB yields have risen, the pension funds have continued to observe the benchmark-portfolio targets set out in their fifth-phase medium-term plan (a five-year plan covering FY2025–FY2029). No material weight changes are evident; with the fifth phase now in its second year, we do not expect a portfolio overhaul in the near term. Even under the current framework, each category is allowed a certain deviation (e.g. the GPIF’s holdings of domestic bonds can be 6pp higher or lower than the targeted 25% share). The funds are scrupulously adhering to the benchmark allocation, yet their monthly rebalancing actions still exert a non-trivial influence on the market. Assuming a monthly rebalancing process, and using the month-to-month index movements from the end of January, a back-of-the- envelope estimate suggests that, to keep each index at its target level by February, the pension funds would need to sell roughly JPY3.2trn of domestic stocks and buy about JPY0.9trn of domestic bonds, JPY1.2trn of foreign bonds, and JPY1.1trn of foreign stocks (see Figure 6). records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 11 Here we note that the statue specifically refers to a balance-of-payments disequilibrium, not a trade deficit. The balance of payments includes both the current account and capital account. The former is comprised primarily of the trade balance, but it also includes primary and secondary income receipts. The capital account includes two components involving capital transactions. The first is net capital transfers and the second is the financial account, which details direct investment, portfolio investment, financial derivatives, reserve assets, and other investment flows. In other words, balance of payments disequilibria are broader than goods trade flows and include capital flows and services trade. Prior to 1973, when much of the world operated under the fixed exchange rate regime of the Bretton Woods system, a balance of payments deficit had a very specific meaning: persistent current account deficits, capital outflows, loss of foreign exchange reserves, and the potential for a forced devaluation (or intervention by the IMF). Because of the fixed exchange rate (with the US dollar pegged to gold acting as the anchor for other currencies), the adjustment occurred through reserve depletion (including gold), domestic contraction, and, in some cases, capital controls. What is the specific plan for 2026? Based on the budget law, the government targets a deficit for the core budget of EUR 98 bn (2.1% of 2026F GDP). This is an increase of about EUR 33 bn (c. 0.7% of 2026F GDP) compared to 2025. Including the off-budgetary SV BW and SV IK the deficit is set to widen by an even stronger EUR 72 bn, totalling about EUR 182 bn (or 3.9% of 2026F GDP). What is more, this deficit expansion is almost entirely due to higher expenditures, which are projected to swell from EUR 538 bn to EUR 608 bn. A breakdown by functional categories shows that the spending increase can be attributed almost entirely to the planned strengthening of defense capabilities and higher investment expenditures. While defense expenditures (core budget & SV BW) are targeted to rise from EUR 87 bn to EUR 119 bn (+ EUR 32 bn), investment spending (core budget & SV IK; excl. the KTF) are planned to increase even more significantly from about EUR 80 bn to roughly EUR 116 bn (+ EUR 37 bn).2 A detailed overview of the 2026 plan figures can be found in Figure 13, Figure 14, and Figure 15 at the end of this report. 1 As our previous work, we take the simplifying assumption that monthly credit flows do match actual spending. records.text: CEIC, Barclays Research Source: Haver Analytics, CEIC, Barclays Research FX and rates strategy: Little solace for Asia FX/rates; idiosyncratic factors in the driving seat Mitul Kotecha Barclays Bank, Singapore | Lemon Zhang Barclays Bank, Singapore | Audrey Ong Barclays Bank, Singapore Asian FX out in the cold, but timing will be important. The USD initially slipped in the wake of the Supreme Court decision to strike down IEEPA tariffs. As we highlighted, we believe the decision is beneficial for risk-sensitive currencies, but we think this mostly applies to high-carry EM FX and G10 currencies with strong fundamentals, rather than relatively lower-yielding Asian currencies. That said, Asia is the biggest trading region and would, on the face of it, benefit would most from a removal of IEEPA tariffs though the administration was quick announce an interim 15% global tariff and new 301 country-specific investigations, which could ultimately be higher. Tariff revenues also may not be affected significantly if enhanced Section 232, Section 301, and Section 122 tariffs are implemented (see Supreme Court strikes down IEEPA tariffs). Therefore, the main issue for Asian markets will be the timing of such measures rather than the overall tariff impact. 23 February 2026 4 Barclays | Emerging Asia
